\chapter{Five More Short Answers}
\label{ch:ml-five-more-short-answers}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can accept, refuse and ask for more or less in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C58-that-will-do and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kūṭutal]{\ml{കൂടുതൽ} (kūṭutal) — more}

\label{lesson:ML-C58-more}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{nakhaṁ} mean, and what did \emph{ellŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കൂടുതൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{കൂടുതൽ}} (\emph{kūṭutal}) — \textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}.

Built on \ml{കൂടുക} (\emph{kūṭuka}), \textquotedblleft{}to join, to gather, to increase\textquotedblright{}, with a tail Malayalam puts on a doing to turn it into a thing. The whole says, roughly, \textquotedblleft{}an increasing\textquotedblright{}.

It answers the question at a Kerala meal, where a server comes round the leaf a second and a third time and the guest has to say something. \ml{കൂടുതൽ} asks for more.

The long \emph{ū} at the front carries the word. Shorten it and you have said something else entirely, so it is worth stretching.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five short answers.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kūṭutal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ellŭ}, then \emph{kūṭutal}, and stretch the long vowel at the front
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കൂടുതൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}more\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṟavŭ]{\ml{കുറവ്} (kuṟavŭ) — less, a shortage}

\label{lesson:ML-C58-less}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kūṭutal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കുറവ്}}
\textbf{\ml{കുറവ്}} (\emph{kuṟavŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}less, a shortage\textquotedblright{}.

The mirror of the last one, built the same way: \ml{കുറയുക} (\emph{kuṟayuka}), \textquotedblleft{}to lessen, to fall short\textquotedblright{}, plus a tail that makes the doing into a thing.

\ml{കുറവ്} is less of something, and it is also a shortfall or a lack. A house short of water has a water \ml{കുറവ്}, and a piece of work with something missing has a \ml{കുറവ്} in it.

The \ml{റ} here is the hard trilled one you met in the rock-word, and the ŭ closes the word the way it closed the root-word and the seed-word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and they are opposites built from the same parts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuṟavŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kūṭutal}, then \emph{kuṟavŭ}, and hear the two tails matching
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കുറവ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}less, a shortage\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṟaccŭ]{\ml{കുറച്ച്} (kuṟaccŭ) — a little, a few}

\label{lesson:ML-C58-a-little}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kuṟavŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കുറച്ച്}}
\textbf{\ml{കുറച്ച്}} (\emph{kuṟaccŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a little, a few\textquotedblright{}.

The same root as the word before it, turned a different way: from \ml{കുറ}-, \textquotedblleft{}to be little\textquotedblright{}, but landing on a quantity rather than on a lack.

The difference matters at a table. \ml{കുറവ്} complains that there is not enough; \ml{കുറച്ച്} politely asks for a small amount. One is a verdict and the other is a request, and they are one syllable apart.

Malayalam gets a great deal out of a single root by varying the tail on it, and this pair is a clean example — the same three sounds at the front, two different jobs at the back.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the last two share a root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuṟaccŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kuṟavŭ}, then \emph{kuṟaccŭ}, and say which of the two you would use asking for rice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കുറച്ച്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a little, a few\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vēṇṭa]{\ml{വേണ്ട} (vēṇṭa) — no need, no thank you}

\label{lesson:ML-C58-no-need}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kuṟaccŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വേണ്ട}}
\textbf{\ml{വേണ്ട}} (\emph{vēṇṭa}) — \textquotedblleft{}no need, no thank you\textquotedblright{}.

The negative partner of \ml{വേണം} (\emph{vēṇaṁ}), \textquotedblleft{}it is wanted\textquotedblright{}. \ml{വേണ്ട} says the opposite: not wanted, not needed, no.

This is the polite refusal at a Kerala meal, and it is said often, because the serving is persistent. Said gently it declines; said firmly it stops the ladle. A guest who has learned only one refusal in Malayalam should learn this one.

Note that it declines the offer rather than the person. Malayalam has warmer ways of saying no to a request, and this one keeps to food, drink and objects.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one gets you through a meal.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vēṇṭa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vēṇṭa}, gently, then \emph{vēṇṭa} again, firmly, and hear the difference the tone makes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വേണ്ട} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}no need, no thank you\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pōruṁ]{\ml{പോരും} (pōruṁ) — that will do, that is enough}

\label{lesson:ML-C58-that-will-do}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vēṇṭa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പോരും}}
\textbf{\ml{പോരും}} (\emph{pōruṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}that will do, that is enough\textquotedblright{}.

From \ml{പോരുക} (\emph{pōruka}), \textquotedblleft{}to suffice\textquotedblright{}, and it means that what is there is already enough.

Set it against \emph{mati}, which you already have. The two overlap, and either will stop a server; \ml{പോരും} leans a little more towards \textquotedblleft{}that reaches far enough\textquotedblright{} and \emph{mati} towards \textquotedblleft{}stop\textquotedblright{}. Kerala uses both, often in the same breath.

The \ml{ം} at the end is the anusvara, the humming close you have met on the sky-word and the star-word and the vessel-word. It closes a great many Malayalam words, and by now it should be arriving without thought.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and you can answer a served plate five ways: more, less, a little, no need, that will do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōruṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{kūṭutal}, \emph{kuṟavŭ}, \emph{kuṟaccŭ}, \emph{vēṇṭa}, \emph{pōruṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പോരും} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}that will do, that is enough\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
